attacks.attack: 1. Re-link the erased commitment without the salt
attacks.detail: even knowing the content, recomputing the commitment needs the 32-byte salt; 1000 trial salts matched=False; the real salt space is 2^256. ACCEPTED LIMIT: if the CONTENT were low-entropy AND the salt known, a salted commitment could be brute-forced — which is why the salt is high-entropy and shredded (non-linkable).
attacks.verdict: DEFENDED (high-entropy salt) + ACCEPTED LIMIT (low-entropy content + known salt would re-link)

attacks.detail: forged cert signed by attacker -> verifies against custodian key=False (rejected); genuine cert verifies=True. ACCEPTED LIMIT: the certificate attests the custodian RAN the erasure workflow — it does not third-party-prove the content is physically gone (needs an independent witness / HSM-enclave attestation, P1+).
attacks.verdict: DEFENDED (forged cert rejected) + ACCEPTED LIMIT (cert attests the WORKFLOW, self-attested)

attacks.attack: 3. Use erasure to silently vanish evidence
attacks.detail: a Certificate of Destruction names the erased ref (ev-004) and time (2026-06-09T14:30:00Z) and is appended permanently; the commitment's inclusion still verifies. You can see THAT (and when) something was erased — just not its content. Erasure cannot be used to make evidence vanish without a trace.
attacks.verdict: DEFENDED — erasure leaves a permanent, auditable tombstone

attacks.detail: dropping the appended cert shrinks the log below the witnessed size; a verifier holding C2 (size 13) rejects a presented log of size 12 -> detected=True.
attacks.verdict: DEFENDED — can't un-append a witnessed certificate

attacks.detail: over-claim hits: none; discloses salted-hash-may-be-personal-data: True; discloses can't-prove-no-copy: True; discloses self-attested-workflow: True.
attacks.verdict: DEFENDED — discloses the legal, no-copy and self-attestation limits
